title: Banach’s Isometric Conjecture over the Complex Field
author: Antonio Acuaviva & Tomasz Kania
abstract: We complete Banach’s isometric conjecture over the complex field. More precisely, if \(X\) is a complex normed space and, for some \(2\leqslant n<\dim_{\mathbb C}X\), all its \(n\)-dimensional complex subspaces are isometric as metric spaces, then the norm is induced by a Hermitian inner product. We also prove the quaternionic counterpart. The central geometric argument first treats real star bodies without convexity or central symmetry; applied to circled complex or quaternionic bodies, it shows that mutually real-linearly equivalent hyperplane sections force the ambient body to be a Hermitian ellipsoid. The proof adapts the bundle-degree mechanism introduced by Lu and Yang for the real case. Finally, we obtain extensions to absolutely homogeneous functions, graded Fréchet spaces, metrisable locally convex spaces, and compatible translation-invariant metrics.

1.

Introduction

−

The question of how much the geometry of a normed space is determined by its subspaces of one fixed finite dimension goes back to Banach. He asked whether a real or complex Banach space \(X\) must be a Hilbert space whenever, for some fixed integer \(2\leqslant n<\dim X\), all its \(n\)-dimensional subspaces are linearly isometric . This is Banach’s isometric conjecture.

Dvoretzky’s theorem settles the conjecture for every fixed \(n\geqslant2\) in infinite-dimensional real Banach spaces , and Milman’s complex version gives the corresponding complex result . The finite-dimensional history is more intricate. Auerbach, Mazur, and Ulam proved the real case \(n=2\) in 1935 . Gromov proved the conjecture for every even \(n\) over \(\mathbb R\) and \(\mathbb C\). For odd \(n\), he also proved it over \(\mathbb R\) when \(\dim_{\mathbb R}X\geqslant n+2\), and over \(\mathbb C\) when \(\dim_{\mathbb C}X\geqslant2n\) .

The bundle approach was subsequently developed by Bor, Hernández-Lamoneda, Jiménez-Desantiago, and Montejano, who proved the real case \(n\equiv1\pmod4\), \(n\geqslant5\), with the possible exception of \(n=133\) . Ivanov, Mamaev, and Nordskova settled the low-dimensional case \(n=3\), \(\dim_{\mathbb R}X=4\) . Most recently, Lu and Yang proved the real conjecture for every odd \(n\), thereby completing the real problem . Their paper is explicitly confined to real spaces. The bundle-degree mechanism used here is theirs, and their construction in turn has the work of Bor et al. as a direct antecedent.

Over \(\mathbb C\), Bracho and Montejano proved the cases \(n\equiv1\pmod4\) . Consequently, before the present work the only residual complex range was \[n\equiv3\pmod4, \qquad n<\dim_{\mathbb C}X<2n.\] The usual two-vector reduction shows that it is enough to consider \(\dim_{\mathbb C}X=n+1\): once every \((n+1)\)-dimensional subspace is Hermitian, the parallelogram identity holds for every pair of vectors. We prove precisely this codimension-one case and hence close the residual range. The quaternionic statement appears to have no antecedent in the literature known to us.

For completeness, Zhang’s recent preprint claims a proof of the full finite-dimensional real problem by means of the John ellipsoid . Its Theorem 3.1 states that an origin-symmetric star body with ellipsoidal hyperplane sections is an ellipsoid. This overlaps the star-body setting but not the implication proved here: our sections are assumed only to be mutually real-linearly equivalent, their ellipsoidality is part of the conclusion, and no central symmetry is imposed. We next establish the complex and quaternionic results considered here, together with several Fréchet-space extensions. To the best of our knowledge, these are not covered by previous results.

The result follows from a statement in which neither convexity nor the triangle inequality is assumed. Throughout the paper, \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb C,\mathbb H\}\). A function \(p\colon X\to[0,\infty)\) is definite if \(p(x)=0\) only for \(x=0\), and it is \(\mathbb F\)-absolutely homogeneous if \(p(xa)=p(x)\lvert a\rvert\) for \(x\in X\) and \(a\in\mathbb F\).

Let \(X\) be a right \(\mathbb F\)-vector space, let \(2\leqslant n<\dim_{\mathbb F}X\), and let \(p\colon X\to[0,\infty)\) be definite and \(\mathbb F\)-absolutely homogeneous. Suppose that

  1. on every \((n+1)\)-dimensional \(\mathbb F\)-subspace \(Y\) of \(X\), the restriction of \(p\) to an auxiliary Euclidean unit sphere is Lipschitz; and

  2. whenever \(E\) and \(F\) are \(n\)-dimensional \(\mathbb F\)-subspaces of \(X\), there is a real-linear bijection \(T\colon E\to F\) such that \(p(Tx)=p(x)\) for every \(x\in E\).

Then there is a positive-definite \(\mathbb F\)-Hermitian form \(h\) on \(X\) such that \(p(x)^2=h(x,x)\) for every \(x\in X\).

No completeness assumption occurs in Theorem A, and only \((n+1)\)-dimensional subspaces are used. The Lipschitz condition is independent of the auxiliary Euclidean structure. Indeed, if \(\lvert \cdot\rvert_1\) and \(\lvert \cdot\rvert_2\) are two Euclidean norms on \(Y\), then the radial identification \[S(Y,\lvert \cdot\rvert_2)\longrightarrow S(Y,\lvert \cdot\rvert_1), \qquad \theta\longmapsto\frac{\theta}{\lvert \theta\rvert_1},\] is smooth and bi-Lipschitz, and absolute homogeneity expresses \(p\) on the first sphere as the product of a smooth positive factor and its restriction to the second. For a norm, condition 1 is automatic. The Mazur–Ulam theorem also shows that the isometries in the following consequence need not be assumed linear, or compatible with multiplication by complex or quaternionic scalars.

Let \(X\) be an \(\mathbb F\)-normed space, and suppose that, for some \(2\leqslant n<\dim_{\mathbb F}X\), all \(n\)-dimensional \(\mathbb F\)-subspaces of \(X\) are bijectively isometric as metric spaces. Then the norm of \(X\) is induced by a positive-definite \(\mathbb F\)-Hermitian form. Consequently, the norm completion of \(X\) is an \(\mathbb F\)-Hilbert space, and \(X\) itself is an \(\mathbb F\)-Hilbert space when it is complete.

For \(\mathbb F=\mathbb C\), the Banach-space case of Corollary B completes the complex conjecture; for \(\mathbb F=\mathbb H\), it gives its quaternionic counterpart. Notice that the proof is dimension-free and obtains the inner product before completion. In particular, the infinite-dimensional quaternionic conclusion does not come from Milman’s complex theorem by restriction of scalars: the quaternionic \(n\)-subspaces form only a proper subfamily of the complex \(2n\)-subspaces.

The geometric statement from which these conclusions follow is likely to be useful independently.

Let \(n\geqslant2\), let \(V\) be a right \(\mathbb F\)-vector space of dimension \(n+1\), and let \(K\subseteq V\) be an \(\mathbb F\)-circled star body with positive Lipschitz radial function. If all central \(\mathbb F\)-hyperplane sections of \(K\) are real-linearly equivalent, then \(K\) is the unit ball of a positive-definite \(\mathbb F\)-Hermitian form.

In the complex case, Theorem 1.1 strengthens the geometric result of Bracho and Montejano in two independent respects: a circled star body replaces a symmetric convex body, and the equivalences between its complex hyperplane sections need only be real-linear. Thus convexity is removed, while circledness is retained for the final scalar reconstruction. The underlying real ellipsoid theorem, Theorem 4.1, requires neither convexity nor central symmetry.

The remaining main results extend this rigidity beyond Banach spaces, first to graded Fréchet spaces and then to vector spaces equipped with a compatible translation-invariant metric. The projective-limit description in Theorem C is standard once the defining seminorms have been shown to be Hilbertian; the substantive assertion is their eventual Hilbertianity. The simultaneous eigenvalue argument in Theorem D gives the stronger conclusion that an entire separating family collapses to one Hermitian norm.

The homogeneous formulation also applies to Fréchet spaces, provided that one fixes either a grading or a compatible translation-invariant metric. Following the graded and multi-seminormed viewpoint of , we shall call an increasing defining sequence \((p_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) reduced \(n\)-isometric if, whenever \(n<\dim_{\mathbb F}(X/\ker p_k)\), all \(n\)-dimensional subspaces of the normed quotient \(X/\ker p_k\) are bijectively isometric. The isometry may depend on \(k\).

Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff Fréchet space over \(\mathbb F\), where \(\dim_{\mathbb F}X>n\geqslant2\). The following assertions are equivalent.

  1. \(X\) admits an increasing defining sequence of Hilbertian seminorms.

  2. \(X\) admits a reduced \(n\)-isometric increasing defining sequence.

For every sequence \((p_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) as in (2), there is \(k_0\in\mathbb N\) such that the cofinal tail \((p_k)_{k\geqslant k_0}\) consists of Hilbertian seminorms, and \[X\cong\varprojlim_{k\geqslant k_0}\widehat{X/\ker p_k},\] where the spaces on the right are \(\mathbb F\)-Hilbert spaces and the canonical bonding maps have dense range.

This conclusion does not imply normability. A stronger conclusion is available when the same map acts at every seminorm level, up to a level-dependent positive factor.

Let \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H\}\). Let \(X\) be a right \(\mathbb F\)-vector space, let \(\mathcal Q\) be a separating family of \(\mathbb F\)-seminorms, and let \(2\leqslant n<\dim_{\mathbb F}X\). Suppose that, for every pair of \(n\)-dimensional subspaces \(E,F\subseteq X\), there is an \(\mathbb F\)-linear isomorphism \(T\colon E\to F\) such that, for each \(p\in\mathcal Q\), there is \(c_p(T)>0\) for which \(p(Tx)=c_p(T)p(x)\) for every \(x\in E\). Then there is a positive-definite \(\mathbb F\)-Hermitian form \(h\) on \(X\) such that every member of \(\mathcal Q\) is either zero or a positive multiple of \(x\mapsto h(x,x)^{1/2}\). Thus \(\mathcal Q\) generates a norm topology; if this topology is complete, then \(X\) is an \(\mathbb F\)-Hilbert space.

A compatible translation-invariant metric gives a third formulation. For such a metric \(d\), put \(B_r^d=\{x:d(x,0)\leqslant r\}\).

Let \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H\}\). Let \(X\) be a Fréchet right \(\mathbb F\)-space, let \(2\leqslant n<\dim_{\mathbb F}X\), and let \(d\) be a compatible translation-invariant metric. Suppose that for every pair of \(n\)-dimensional \(\mathbb F\)-subspaces \(E,F\subseteq X\), there is an \(\mathbb F\)-linear bijection \(T\colon E\to F\) satisfying \[d(Tx,Ty)=d(x,y) \qquad(x,y\in E).\] Suppose also that there is a set \(\mathcal R\subseteq(0,\infty)\), with \(0\in\overline{\mathcal R}\), for which one of the following assertions holds.

  1. Every \(B_r^d\), \(r\in\mathcal R\), is \(\mathbb F\)-absolutely convex.

  2. For every \(r\in\mathcal R\) and every finite-dimensional \(\mathbb F\)-subspace \(W\subseteq X\), the section \(B_r^d\cap W\) is a compact \(\mathbb F\)-circled star body in \(W\) with positive Lipschitz radial function.

If \(\mathbb F=\mathbb R\) and assertion (2) is used, assume in addition that \(n\) is odd. Then a positive-definite \(\mathbb F\)-Hermitian form on \(X\) induces the original topology, and \(X\) is an \(\mathbb F\)-Hilbert space. If every closed centred \(d\)-ball is \(\mathbb F\)-absolutely convex, the corresponding norm may be chosen so that \[d(x,y)=\phi\bigl(\lVert x-y\rVert\bigr),\] where \(\phi\colon[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) is non-decreasing and subadditive, vanishes at \(0\), and is strictly positive on \((0,\infty)\).

The proof starts from the Lipschitz bundle-degree argument of Lu and Yang , developed there for origin-symmetric convex bodies and their hyperplane sections. Mutually equivalent sections determine a principal bundle of exact section maps. After reduction to the identity component, a self-map of the parameter sphere of positive degree annihilates the bundle class. A Lipschitz trivialisation then gives an exact family to which the signed degree formula applies. It follows that two consecutive even powers of Minkowski’s functional of a reference section are polynomials; unique factorisation makes its square quadratic. The real ambient dimensions and the relevant homotopy-group indices have the required parity over both \(\mathbb C\) and \(\mathbb H\). A final polarisation argument recovers the scalar structure. We give the details needed to pass from origin-symmetric convex bodies and hyperplane sections to possibly non-convex star bodies and the more general section fields used below.

2.

Preliminaries

−

We write \(\mathbb N=\{1,2,\ldots\}\). Euclidean structures, adjoints, tensor products, and measures are real unless a scalar field is indicated. Vector spaces over \(\mathbb F\) are right modules. An \(\mathbb F\)-Hermitian form is conjugate-linear in the first variable and right-linear in the second; for \(\mathbb H\) we use the conventions of . A set \(K\) is \(\mathbb F\)-circled if \(Ka=K\) whenever \(a\in\mathbb F\) and \(\lvert a\rvert=1\).

An \(\mathbb F\)-seminorm \(p\) is Hilbertian if \(p(x)^2=h(x,x)\) for a positive-semidefinite \(\mathbb F\)-Hermitian form \(h\). Its radical is then \(\ker p\). When \(h\) is positive definite, we also call \(p\) a Hermitian norm. Completeness is not part of this terminology. A graded Fréchet space is a Fréchet space with a fixed increasing defining sequence of seminorms. A subset \(C\) of a right \(\mathbb F\)-vector space is \(\mathbb F\)-absolutely convex if \(xa+yb\in C\) whenever \(x,y\in C\) and \(\lvert a\rvert+\lvert b\rvert\leqslant1\).

Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real Euclidean space, with closed unit ball \(B_V\) and unit sphere \(S(V)\). A star body about the origin is a set \[ K=\{t\theta:\theta\in S(V),\ 0\leqslant t\leqslant\rho_K(\theta)\}, \](1) where \(\rho_K\colon S(V)\to(0,\infty)\) is continuous. Minkowski’s functional of \(K\) is \(p_K(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tK\}\). Thus \(p_K(0)=0\) and \(p_K(x)=\lvert x\rvert/\rho_K(x/\lvert x\rvert)\) for \(x\neq0\); it need not be a norm.

If \(\rho_K\) is Lipschitz, then so is \(p_K\). Indeed, put \(f=1/\rho_K\), and let \(M=\sup f\) and \(L=\operatorname{Lip}(f)\). If \(0<\lvert x\rvert\leqslant\lvert y\rvert\), then \(\lvert x\rvert\lvert x/\lvert x\rvert-y/\lvert y\rvert\rvert\leqslant2\lvert x-y\rvert\), and consequently \[ \lvert p_K(x)-p_K(y)\rvert\leqslant(M+2L)\lvert x-y\rvert. \](2) The cases in which one of the vectors is zero follow directly. No convexity is required for this estimate.

Let \(E\) be an \(m\)-dimensional real Euclidean space and let \(S\subseteq E\) be a star body. Its normalised covariance is the positive operator \(C(S)=\operatorname{vol}(S)^{-1}\int_S x\otimes x\,dx\). For every real-linear isomorphism \(T\), change of variables gives \[ C(TS)=TC(S)T^*. \](3) In particular, applying \(C(S)^{-1/2}\) puts \(S\) in covariance position, where \(C(S)= \mathrm{Id}\).

The covariance here is deliberately taken about the prescribed origin, not about the barycentre. The origin is part of the star-body structure and is fixed by every linear equivalence under consideration. Positivity of \(C(S)\) uses only that \(S\) contains a neighbourhood of the origin: for \(v\neq0\), the function \(x\mapsto(x,v)_{\mathbb R}\) is nonzero on an open subset of \(S\), and hence \((C(S)v,v)_{\mathbb R}>0\). Neither central symmetry nor convexity is involved.

For \(j\geqslant1\), put \(M_j(S)=\operatorname{vol}(S)^{-1}\int_Sx^{\otimes j}\,dx\in\operatorname{Sym}^j(E)\). Then \(M_j(TS)=T^{\otimes j}M_j(S)\). Polar coordinates give \[ \operatorname{vol}(S)=\frac1m\int_{S(E)}\rho_S(\theta)^m\,d\theta, \qquad M_j(S)=\frac{m}{m+j}\, \frac{\int_{S(E)}\rho_S(\theta)^{m+j}\theta^{\otimes j}\,d\theta} {\int_{S(E)}\rho_S(\theta)^m\,d\theta}. \](4) It follows that, on any family with common positive inner and finite outer radii, each fixed moment depends Lipschitz-continuously on the radial function in the uniform norm.

The next lemma combines two results of Lu and Yang . In their centrally symmetric setting, the odd moments vanish. In the present setting, the odd moments need not vanish, and the same finite-generation argument simply selects whichever even or odd degrees are required. Neither the covariance normalisation nor the moment and stabiliser arguments use convexity. Thus the proof applies to Lipschitz star bodies about the origin.

Suppose that \(C(S)= \mathrm{Id}\), and put \(G=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb R}(S)=\{g\in\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbb R}(E):gS=S\}\). Then:

  1. \(G\) is a compact subgroup of \(O(E)\).

  2. There are positive integers \(j_1,\ldots,j_s\) such that \(G\) is exactly the stabiliser in \(O(E)\) of the tuple \(M(S)=(M_{j_1}(S),\ldots,M_{j_s}(S))\).

  3. The orbit map \(O(E)/G\to O(E)M(S)\), given by \(QG\mapsto QM(S)\), is a diffeomorphism onto a compact embedded submanifold, and its inverse is locally Lipschitz for the ambient Euclidean distance.

ProofFold proof

Proof. The proof of (1) is verbatim that of : from \(C(S)=\mathrm{Id}\), every \(g\in G\) satisfies \(gg^*=\mathrm{Id}\), and \(G\) is a closed subgroup of \(O(E)\), hence compact.

For (2), the same argument requires only one minor modification. In the centrally symmetric setting of Lu and Yang the odd moments vanish, whereas here \(S\) need not satisfy \(S=-S\). We therefore retain the full sequence \((M_j(S))_{j\geqslant1}\). Every member of \(G\) fixes every moment of \(S\). Conversely, suppose that \(Q\in O(E)\) fixes \(M_j(S)\) for every \(j\geqslant1\). The normalised uniform measures on \(S\) and \(QS\) then have the same integral against every polynomial. By the Stone–Weierstrass theorem, they agree on \(C(S\cup QS)\), and hence are equal. Since their supports are \(S\) and \(QS\), respectively, it follows that \(QS=S\).

Finally, the equations \(Q^{\otimes j}M_j(S)=M_j(S)\), \(j\geqslant1\), are polynomial equations in the matrix entries of \(Q\). The Hilbert basis theorem therefore reduces this family to finitely many degrees \(j_1,\ldots,j_s\), whose common stabiliser in \(O(E)\) is still exactly \(G\). This proves (2).

With this finite moment tuple in hand, the proof of (3) is verbatim that of . ◻

3.

Polynomial rigidity

−

We use the standard conventions for Brouwer degree and for the degree of maps between oriented spheres, as in . The following theorem records the form of the degree calculation of Lu and Yang needed below. Their degree argument extends to star bodies and positively homogeneous functions. The only point in their proof where convexity is used is in Lemma 4.4, through their Lemma 2.1, to ensure that \(\partial K\) has zero ambient measure. For a star body with Lipschitz radial function, this follows instead because \(\theta\mapsto\rho_K(\theta)\theta\) is a Lipschitz map from \(S(V)\) onto \(\partial K\). Central symmetry is not used in the degree calculation; its earlier role was only to annihilate odd moments, a point already handled in Lemma 2.1 by retaining moments of every positive degree. We include the details for completeness.

Let \(V\) be an oriented real Euclidean space of dimension \(N>0\), let \(E\) be a nonzero finite-dimensional real vector space equipped with an auxiliary Euclidean structure, let \(K\subseteq V\) be a star body, and let \(p\colon E\to[0,\infty)\). Suppose that:

  1. \(N\) is even;

  2. the radial function of \(K\) is Lipschitz;

  3. \(p\) is positive away from the origin and positively homogeneous;

  4. there are a continuous map \(\varphi\colon S(V)\to S(V)\), with \(\deg\varphi\neq0\), and a Lipschitz map \(A\colon S(V)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(E,V)\);

  5. the identities \[ (A_zy,\varphi(z))_{\mathbb R}=0 \quad\hbox{and}\quad p_K(A_zy)=p(y) \qquad(z\in S(V),\ y\in E) \](5) hold.

Then \(p^{N+2k}\) is a real homogeneous polynomial for every \(k\geqslant0\). In particular, \(p^2\) is a positive-definite real quadratic form.

ProofFold proof

Proof. Put \(D=\deg\varphi\), which is nonzero by (4). Extend \(A\) homogeneously to \(B_V\) by setting \(\mathcal A(0)=0\) and \(\mathcal A(tz)=tA_z\) for \(0<t\leqslant1\) and \(z\in S(V)\). The Lipschitz property in (4) shows that this extension is Lipschitz. Indeed, if \(L_0=\sup_z\lVert A_z\rVert\), \(L_1=\operatorname{Lip}(A)\), \(x=\lambda z\), \(x'=\mu w\), and \(0\leqslant\lambda\leqslant\mu\leqslant1\), then \[\lVert \lambda A_z-\mu A_w\rVert \leqslant \lambda L_1\lvert z-w\rvert+L_0\lvert \lambda-\mu\rvert \leqslant (2L_1+L_0)\lvert x-x'\rvert.\] Here we used \(\lambda\lvert z-w\rvert\leqslant2\lvert x-x'\rvert\) and \(\lvert \lambda-\mu\rvert\leqslant\lvert x-x'\rvert\); the same estimate covers the origin.

Fix \(y\neq0\) and put \(r=p(y)>0\), where positivity follows from (3). Define \(F_y(x)=\mathcal A(x)y\) for \(x\in B_V\) and \(w_y(z)=A_zy/\lvert A_zy\rvert\) for \(z\in S(V)\). The second identity in (5) ensures that \(A_zy\neq0\). By the first identity in (5), the unit vectors \(\varphi(z)\) and \(w_y(z)\) are orthogonal, so \[(z,t)\longmapsto \cos(\pi t/2)\varphi(z)+\sin(\pi t/2)w_y(z) \qquad(0\leqslant t\leqslant1)\] is a homotopy through the unit sphere. Hence \(\deg w_y=D\).

The second identity in (5) also gives \(A_zy\in r\partial K\). The radial homeomorphism \(\widehat\Psi_r(t\theta)=tr\rho_K(\theta)\theta\), for \(t\geqslant0\), is joined to the identity by the positive radial interpolation \(t\theta\mapsto t((1-s)+sr\rho_K(\theta))\theta\). It is therefore orientation preserving and maps \(B_V\) onto \(rK\). If \(Cw_y(tz)=tw_y(z)\) denotes the cone on \(w_y\), then \(F_y=\widehat\Psi_r\circ Cw_y\). The boundary characterisation and composition rule for Brouwer degree consequently give \[ \deg(F_y,\operatorname{int}B_V,v)=D \quad\hbox{for }v\in\operatorname{int}(rK), \](6) whereas the degree is zero for \(v\notin rK\), since \(F_y(B_V)\subseteq rK\). No smoothness of \(\partial K\) is involved.

Let \(\Omega=\operatorname{int}B_V\). The coordinatewise McShane theorem extends \(F_y\) from the closed ball to a Lipschitz map \(\widetilde F_y\) on \(V\). The extension agrees with \(F_y\) on \(\Omega\), and therefore has the same derivative almost everywhere there. We spell out the measure-theoretic hypotheses of the signed degree formula. Every Lipschitz map between \(N\)-dimensional Euclidean spaces has the Lusin \((N)\) property: if \(A\) has measure zero, then the standard Hausdorff-measure estimate \[\mathcal H^N(\widetilde F_y(A)) \leqslant \operatorname{Lip}(\widetilde F_y)^N\mathcal H^N(A)\] shows that its image has measure zero. Moreover, by (2), \(\partial K\) is the Lipschitz image of the \((N-1)\)-sphere under \(\theta\mapsto\rho_K(\theta)\theta\), so it has \(N\)-dimensional measure zero. Since \(F_y(\partial\Omega)\subseteq r\partial K\), the image of the boundary is null. Rademacher’s theorem provides the derivative almost everywhere; on the bounded set \(\Omega\), its determinant is integrable because \(\widetilde F_y\) is Lipschitz.

Choose \(\chi\in C_c(V)\) which is one on a neighbourhood of \(rK\), and put \(g(v)=\chi(v)\lvert v\rvert^{2k}\), interpreting \(\lvert v\rvert^0\) as one. The function \(g\) is bounded and compactly supported. Thus all the hypotheses of the signed area–degree formula are satisfied by \(\widetilde F_y\), \(\Omega\), and \(g\). As \(\widetilde F_y=F_y\) on \(\Omega\), (6) gives \[ \int_\Omega\lvert F_y(x)\rvert^{2k}\det_{\mathbb R}DF_y(x)\,dx =D\int_{rK}\lvert v\rvert^{2k}\,dv \notag =D\,p(y)^{N+2k}\int_K\lvert u\rvert^{2k}\,du. \](3)

Regard \(\mathcal A\colon\Omega\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(E,V)\) as a Lipschitz map between Euclidean spaces. Rademacher’s theorem supplies a single null set \(Z\subseteq\Omega\), independent of \(y\), outside which \(\mathcal A\) is differentiable. If \(h_1,\ldots,h_N\) is an oriented orthonormal basis of \(V\), then \(DF_y(x)[h_j]=(D\mathcal A(x)[h_j])y\) for \(x\notin Z\). Each column of the Jacobian is real-linear in \(y\), and hence its determinant is a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(N\) in \(y\). Moreover, \(\lvert F_y(x)\rvert^{2k}=(\mathcal A(x)y,\mathcal A(x)y)_{\mathbb R}^{k}\) is a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(2k\). Both \(\mathcal A\) and \(D\mathcal A\) are essentially bounded, so every coefficient of the resulting polynomial integrand is bounded by an integrable constant on \(\Omega\). The left-hand side of (3) is consequently a homogeneous polynomial \(P_k(y)\) of degree \(N+2k\). The constant \(D\int_K\lvert u\rvert^{2k}\,du\) is nonzero because \(D\neq0\) by (4) and \(K\) has positive volume. Thus \(p^{N+2k}=P_k/(D\int_K\lvert u\rvert^{2k}\,du)\) away from zero, and hence everywhere by (3).

It remains to use (1). Write \(N=2a\), and let \(P=p^{2a}\) and \(Q=p^{2a+2}\), which are nonzero homogeneous polynomials by what we have just proved. Pointwise, and therefore as a polynomial identity, \(Q^a=P^{a+1}\). For each irreducible polynomial \(\pi\), unique factorisation gives \(a\nu_\pi(Q)=(a+1)\nu_\pi(P)\). Since \(a\) and \(a+1\) are coprime, there is an integer \(\ell_\pi\geqslant0\) such that \(\nu_\pi(P)=a\ell_\pi\) and \(\nu_\pi(Q)=(a+1)\ell_\pi\). Thus \(P\) divides \(Q\). The quotient \(R=Q/P\) is homogeneous of degree two and satisfies \(R(y)=p(y)^2\) for \(y\neq0\), hence also at zero. By (3), \(R\) is positive away from zero, and therefore it is a positive-definite real quadratic form. ◻

4.

Spherical sections and exact families

−

The preceding theorem turns a nonzero-degree exact family into an ellipsoid. We next show that mutually equivalent spherical sections provide such a family.

Let \(V\) be an oriented real Euclidean space of even dimension \(N\geqslant4\), let \(1\leqslant d\leqslant N-1\), and let \(u\mapsto H_u\) be a smooth map from \(S(V)\) to the Grassmannian \(\operatorname{Gr}_d(V)\), with \(H_u\subseteq u^\perp\) for every \(u\). Let \(K\subseteq V\) be a star body with positive Lipschitz radial function. If the sections \(K\cap H_u\) are mutually real-linearly equivalent, then every one of them is a real ellipsoid. If, in addition, every pair of vectors in \(V\) belongs to some \(H_u\), then \(K\) is a real ellipsoid.

No injectivity of \(u\mapsto H_u\) is assumed or used. In the complex and quaternionic applications the parametrisation is necessarily redundant: \(H_{ua}=H_u\) whenever \(\lvert a\rvert=1\). Working over the full sphere is precisely what provides the normal vector required by the degree argument.

For the remainder of this section, let \(\Sigma=S(V)\) and put \(S_u=K\cap H_u\). The construction is real; the complex and quaternionic structures enter only in Section 5. We use the standard terminology for principal bundles, local sections, transition functions, pullbacks, and reductions of structure group, with the conventions of . By a finite Lipschitz atlas we mean a finite trivialising cover whose local sections and transition functions are Lipschitz.

Let us fix \(u_0\in\Sigma\), put \(E=H_{u_0}\), and choose a reference body \(S\subseteq E\) equivalent to every \(S_u\). After a real-linear change of coordinates, we may suppose that \(C(S)= \mathrm{Id}\). Put \(G=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb R}(S)\) and, for \(u\in\Sigma\), \[\mathcal P_u=\{A\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(E,V):A(E)=H_u,\ A(S)=S_u\}.\] Right composition by \(G\) is free and transitive on each \(\mathcal P_u\). We now assemble these sets into a principal bundle.

An isometric homogeneity condition on a Fréchet space requires more than its locally convex topology: one must fix either a defining sequence of seminorms or a compatible translation-invariant metric. Linear homeomorphism of finite-dimensional subspaces alone carries no information, since every finite-dimensional Hausdorff topological vector space over \(\mathbb F\) has its usual Euclidean topology. Since \(\mathcal Q\) is separating, it contains a nonzero member, and the topology generated by \(\mathcal Q\) is precisely its norm topology. If this topology is complete, that Hermitian norm is complete. ◻

A compatible translation-invariant metric determines the family of its centred balls, and every linear \(d\)-isometry preserves each ball together with Minkowski’s functional associated with it.

Proof of Theorem EFold proof

Proof of Theorem E. Let us fix \(x_0\neq0\) and replace \(\mathcal R\) by \(\{r\in\mathcal R:r<d(x_0,0)\}\). It still has zero in its closure, and every corresponding ball is proper. Each \(B_r^d\) is closed and contains the open ball of radius \(r\), so it is a neighbourhood of zero and hence is absorbing. If \(T\colon E\to F\) is one of the linear \(d\)-isometries, then \(T0=0\) and \[T(B_r^d\cap E)=B_r^d\cap F \qquad(r\in\mathcal R).\] Thus the same map preserves Minkowski’s functional associated with every ball considered below.

Suppose first that the balls are \(\mathbb F\)-absolutely convex. For \(r\in\mathcal R\), put \(p_r(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tB_r^d\}\). Since \(B_r^d\) is closed, absolutely convex, and absorbing, \(p_r\) is a continuous \(\mathbb F\)-seminorm and \(B_r^d=\{x:p_r(x)\leqslant1\}\). The family \(\{p_r:r\in\mathcal R\}\) is separating: if \(x\neq0\), choose \(r<d(x,0)\), so that \(x\notin B_r^d\). It generates the original topology because the balls with \(r\in\mathcal R\) form a neighbourhood basis at zero. Every linear \(d\)-isometry preserves every \(p_r\). The case \(c_p(T)=1\) of Theorem D shows that the nonzero \(p_r\)’s are positive multiples of a single Hermitian norm \(q\). Consequently, \(q\) induces the original Fréchet topology and is complete.

Suppose next that the finite-dimensional sections are Lipschitz star bodies, and define \(p_r\) by the same infimum. If \(W\) is finite-dimensional, then \(p_r|_W\) is Minkowski’s functional of \(B_r^d\cap W\). Taking \(W=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F}\{x\}\) shows that \(p_r(x)\) is finite and positive for \(x\neq0\), and the circled radial structure gives \(p_r(xa)=p_r(x)\lvert a\rvert\). Closedness gives \(B_r^d=\{x:p_r(x)\leqslant1\}\). The radial regularity says precisely that \(p_r\) is Lipschitz on an auxiliary Euclidean sphere in every finite-dimensional subspace. Since every linear \(d\)-isometry preserves \(p_r\), Theorem A makes each \(p_r\) a Hermitian norm when \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb C,\mathbb H\}\). When \(\mathbb F=\mathbb R\), the additional assumption that \(n\) is odd allows the same conclusion by applying Theorem 4.1 on every \((n+1)\)-dimensional subspace and then using the parallelogram identity. The family is separating as above, and the field-independent Theorem D shows that its members are proportional. Their unit balls form a neighbourhood basis, so the resulting Hermitian norm induces the original topology and is complete.

Finally, suppose that every closed centred \(d\)-ball is \(\mathbb F\)-absolutely convex. Apply the first part to Minkowski’s functional of each proper ball. There is a fixed Hermitian norm \(q\) for which every proper \(B_r^d\) is a scalar multiple of the \(q\)-unit ball; nonproper balls are all of \(X\). Vectors with the same \(q\)-norm therefore belong to exactly the same closed \(d\)-balls. Since \(d(x,0)=\inf\{r\geqslant0:x\in B_r^d\}\), they have the same distance from zero. Hence \(d(x,y)=\phi(q(x-y))\) for a non-decreasing function \(\phi\) which vanishes only at zero. If \(e\) is a \(q\)-unit vector, translation invariance and the triangle inequality give \[\phi(s+t)=d((s+t)e,0) \leqslant d(se,0)+d(te,0) =\phi(s)+\phi(t),\] so \(\phi\) is subadditive. ◻

The Fréchet hypothesis is used only for completeness. For a Hausdorff metrisable locally convex space satisfying the other assumptions, the same argument produces a Hermitian norm which induces the topology, and the completion is Hilbert. The real version is included in Theorem E: absolutely convex balls give the conclusion for every \(n\geqslant2\), using the real Banach theorem at each level, whereas the star-body alternative is asserted for odd \(n\), the parity range of Theorem 4.1.

The convex-ball hypothesis occurs for a standard class of compatible metrics. Let \((q_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}\) be a separating increasing sequence of \(\mathbb F\)-seminorms defining a Fréchet topology, and put \[d_0(x,y)=\sup_{j\geqslant1}2^{-j} \frac{q_j(x-y)}{1+q_j(x-y)}.\] The function \(t\mapsto t/(1+t)\) is increasing and subadditive, so \(d_0\) is a translation-invariant metric. It induces the original topology: the finitely many terms with small index control any prescribed finite collection of seminorms, while the remaining terms are uniformly bounded by \(2^{-j}\). The same finite-head and uniform-tail argument shows completeness: a \(d_0\)-Cauchy sequence is Cauchy for each \(q_j\), hence converges in the Fréchet space, and then converges for \(d_0\). Moreover, \[B_r^{d_0} =\bigcap_{2^{-j}>r} \left\{x:q_j(x)\leqslant\frac{r}{2^{-j}-r}\right\},\] so every closed ball is \(\mathbb F\)-absolutely convex, and any linear map preserving every \(q_j\) preserves \(d_0\). The theorem nevertheless concerns the chosen metric: invariance of the Fréchet topology alone does not imply invariance of its centred balls.

results.statementHtml:
Let \(X\) be a right \(\mathbb F\)-vector space, let \(2\leqslant n<\dim_{\mathbb F}X\), and let \(p\colon X\to[0,\infty)\) be definite and \(\mathbb F\)-absolutely homogeneous. Suppose that

  1. on every \((n+1)\)-dimensional \(\mathbb F\)-subspace \(Y\) of \(X\), the restriction of \(p\) to an auxiliary Euclidean unit sphere is Lipschitz; and

  2. whenever \(E\) and \(F\) are \(n\)-dimensional \(\mathbb F\)-subspaces of \(X\), there is a real-linear bijection \(T\colon E\to F\) such that \(p(Tx)=p(x)\) for every \(x\in E\).

Then there is a positive-definite \(\mathbb F\)-Hermitian form \(h\) on \(X\) such that \(p(x)^2=h(x,x)\) for every \(x\in X\).

Let \(X\) be an \(\mathbb F\)-normed space, and suppose that, for some \(2\leqslant n<\dim_{\mathbb F}X\), all \(n\)-dimensional \(\mathbb F\)-subspaces of \(X\) are bijectively isometric as metric spaces. Then the norm of \(X\) is induced by a positive-definite \(\mathbb F\)-Hermitian form. Consequently, the norm completion of \(X\) is an \(\mathbb F\)-Hilbert space, and \(X\) itself is an \(\mathbb F\)-Hilbert space when it is complete.

Let \(n\geqslant2\), let \(V\) be a right \(\mathbb F\)-vector space of dimension \(n+1\), and let \(K\subseteq V\) be an \(\mathbb F\)-circled star body with positive Lipschitz radial function. If all central \(\mathbb F\)-hyperplane sections of \(K\) are real-linearly equivalent, then \(K\) is the unit ball of a positive-definite \(\mathbb F\)-Hermitian form.

Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff Fréchet space over \(\mathbb F\), where \(\dim_{\mathbb F}X>n\geqslant2\). The following assertions are equivalent.

  1. \(X\) admits an increasing defining sequence of Hilbertian seminorms.

  2. \(X\) admits a reduced \(n\)-isometric increasing defining sequence.

For every sequence \((p_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) as in (2), there is \(k_0\in\mathbb N\) such that the cofinal tail \((p_k)_{k\geqslant k_0}\) consists of Hilbertian seminorms, and \[X\cong\varprojlim_{k\geqslant k_0}\widehat{X/\ker p_k},\] where the spaces on the right are \(\mathbb F\)-Hilbert spaces and the canonical bonding maps have dense range.

Let \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H\}\). Let \(X\) be a right \(\mathbb F\)-vector space, let \(\mathcal Q\) be a separating family of \(\mathbb F\)-seminorms, and let \(2\leqslant n<\dim_{\mathbb F}X\). Suppose that, for every pair of \(n\)-dimensional subspaces \(E,F\subseteq X\), there is an \(\mathbb F\)-linear isomorphism \(T\colon E\to F\) such that, for each \(p\in\mathcal Q\), there is \(c_p(T)>0\) for which \(p(Tx)=c_p(T)p(x)\) for every \(x\in E\). Then there is a positive-definite \(\mathbb F\)-Hermitian form \(h\) on \(X\) such that every member of \(\mathcal Q\) is either zero or a positive multiple of \(x\mapsto h(x,x)^{1/2}\). Thus \(\mathcal Q\) generates a norm topology; if this topology is complete, then \(X\) is an \(\mathbb F\)-Hilbert space.

Let \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H\}\). Let \(X\) be a Fréchet right \(\mathbb F\)-space, let \(2\leqslant n<\dim_{\mathbb F}X\), and let \(d\) be a compatible translation-invariant metric. Suppose that for every pair of \(n\)-dimensional \(\mathbb F\)-subspaces \(E,F\subseteq X\), there is an \(\mathbb F\)-linear bijection \(T\colon E\to F\) satisfying \[d(Tx,Ty)=d(x,y) \qquad(x,y\in E).\] Suppose also that there is a set \(\mathcal R\subseteq(0,\infty)\), with \(0\in\overline{\mathcal R}\), for which one of the following assertions holds.

  1. Every \(B_r^d\), \(r\in\mathcal R\), is \(\mathbb F\)-absolutely convex.

  2. For every \(r\in\mathcal R\) and every finite-dimensional \(\mathbb F\)-subspace \(W\subseteq X\), the section \(B_r^d\cap W\) is a compact \(\mathbb F\)-circled star body in \(W\) with positive Lipschitz radial function.

If \(\mathbb F=\mathbb R\) and assertion (2) is used, assume in addition that \(n\) is odd. Then a positive-definite \(\mathbb F\)-Hermitian form on \(X\) induces the original topology, and \(X\) is an \(\mathbb F\)-Hilbert space. If every closed centred \(d\)-ball is \(\mathbb F\)-absolutely convex, the corresponding norm may be chosen so that \[d(x,y)=\phi\bigl(\lVert x-y\rVert\bigr),\] where \(\phi\colon[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) is non-decreasing and subadditive, vanishes at \(0\), and is strictly positive on \((0,\infty)\).

Suppose that \(C(S)= \mathrm{Id}\), and put \(G=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb R}(S)=\{g\in\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbb R}(E):gS=S\}\). Then:

  1. \(G\) is a compact subgroup of \(O(E)\).

  2. There are positive integers \(j_1,\ldots,j_s\) such that \(G\) is exactly the stabiliser in \(O(E)\) of the tuple \(M(S)=(M_{j_1}(S),\ldots,M_{j_s}(S))\).

  3. The orbit map \(O(E)/G\to O(E)M(S)\), given by \(QG\mapsto QM(S)\), is a diffeomorphism onto a compact embedded submanifold, and its inverse is locally Lipschitz for the ambient Euclidean distance.

Let \(V\) be an oriented real Euclidean space of dimension \(N>0\), let \(E\) be a nonzero finite-dimensional real vector space equipped with an auxiliary Euclidean structure, let \(K\subseteq V\) be a star body, and let \(p\colon E\to[0,\infty)\). Suppose that:

  1. \(N\) is even;

  2. the radial function of \(K\) is Lipschitz;

  3. \(p\) is positive away from the origin and positively homogeneous;

  4. there are a continuous map \(\varphi\colon S(V)\to S(V)\), with \(\deg\varphi\neq0\), and a Lipschitz map \(A\colon S(V)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(E,V)\);

  5. the identities \[ (A_zy,\varphi(z))_{\mathbb R}=0 \quad\hbox{and}\quad p_K(A_zy)=p(y) \qquad(z\in S(V),\ y\in E) \](5) hold.

Then \(p^{N+2k}\) is a real homogeneous polynomial for every \(k\geqslant0\). In particular, \(p^2\) is a positive-definite real quadratic form.

Let \(V\) be an oriented real Euclidean space of even dimension \(N\geqslant4\), let \(1\leqslant d\leqslant N-1\), and let \(u\mapsto H_u\) be a smooth map from \(S(V)\) to the Grassmannian \(\operatorname{Gr}_d(V)\), with \(H_u\subseteq u^\perp\) for every \(u\). Let \(K\subseteq V\) be a star body with positive Lipschitz radial function. If the sections \(K\cap H_u\) are mutually real-linearly equivalent, then every one of them is a real ellipsoid. If, in addition, every pair of vectors in \(V\) belongs to some \(H_u\), then \(K\) is a real ellipsoid.

For every \(u_*\in\Sigma\), there is a connected neighbourhood \(U\) of \(u_*\) and a Lipschitz map \(u\mapsto A_u\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(E,V)\) such that \(A_u(E)=H_u\) and \(A_u(S)=S_u\). Finitely many such maps may be chosen so that the transition functions into \(G\) are Lipschitz on their overlaps. Consequently, \(\mathcal P=\coprod_{u\in\Sigma}\mathcal P_u\to\Sigma\) is a principal \(G\)-bundle with a finite Lipschitz atlas.

The bundle \(\mathcal P\) contains a principal \(G^\circ\)-subbundle \(\mathcal P^\circ\) with a finite Lipschitz atlas. Moreover, there are \(D\geqslant1\) and a smooth map \(\varphi\colon S^{N-1}\to S^{N-1}\) of degree \(D\) such that \(\varphi^*\mathcal P^\circ\) is topologically trivial.

Let \(M\) be a compact smooth manifold, let \(L\subseteq O(q)\) be compact, and let \(P\to M\) be a topologically trivial principal \(L\)-bundle with a finite Lipschitz atlas. Then \(P\) has a global Lipschitz section.

There are a smooth map \(\varphi\colon S^{N-1}\to S^{N-1}\) of positive degree and a Lipschitz map \(z\mapsto A_z\) from \(S^{N-1}\) to \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(E,V)\) such that \[ A_z(E)=H_{\varphi(z)} \quad\hbox{and}\quad A_z(S)=K\cap H_{\varphi(z)} \](7) for every \(z\in S^{N-1}\).

Let \(E\) be a right \(\mathbb F\)-vector space, and let \(q\) be a positive-definite real quadratic form on \(E_{\mathbb R}\) such that \(q(xa)=q(x)\lvert a\rvert^2\) for \(x\in E\) and \(a\in\mathbb F\). Then there is a unique positive-definite \(\mathbb F\)-Hermitian form \(h\) with \(h(x,x)=q(x)\).

theorem-a.label: Complex case
theorem-a.note: Lean proves that the square of the original homogeneous function is the diagonal of a positive Hermitian form, over both the complex and quaternionic fields. The proof uses the vanishing of the rational homology class of the clutching map.

corollary-b.label: Complex norm
corollary-b.note: The hypotheses use bijective metric isometries of the subspaces. The proofs identify the original norm with the norm of a Hermitian form and give the Hilbert space conclusions for the completion and for an already complete space.

theorem-1-1.note: There is no separate Lean proof linked for this passage.

theorem-c.label: Complex grading equivalence
theorem-c.note: For both scalar fields, Lean proves the equivalence between Hilbertian and reduced isometric gradings. The proofs of the cofinal Hilbert inverse limit use the actual quotient norms and the canonical bonding maps with dense range.

theorem-d.label: Complex proportionality
theorem-d.note: For each pair of subspaces, one linear equivalence works for the whole family of seminorms. Lean proves proportionality, including the zero alternative, and the norm and Hilbert space conclusions over all three scalar fields.

theorem-e.label: Complex Hilbert space
theorem-e.note: The proofs retain the original translation-invariant distance and both ball hypotheses. For real spaces, odd section dimension is required in the circled star-body case. The profile declarations express the original distance in terms of the Hilbert norm when every closed centred ball is absolutely convex.
